tasks.task_description: Subproblem (a): build a model of passenger flow through a single airport security checkpoint, identify the bottlenecks and problem areas in the current process, using the supplied single-day dataset (Pre-Check and Regular arrivals plus ID-check, millimeter-wave, X-ray and belt-retrieval service timestamps).
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: a discrete-event queueing simulation of one checkpoint, treating each physical stage as a server (or server pool) that passengers queue for. The current layout (Problem Fig.1) has four serial/parallel service stages per passenger: (A) ID/document check by an officer; (B) walk to the open screening line and prepare belongings (shoes, belt, jacket, metal, electronics, liquids, laptops) into bins at the belt; (C) the bag line — bins travel the conveyor through the X-ray (Zone D flags some bags for manual search); (D) the body line — the passenger goes through a millimeter-wave scanner or metal detector, failing a fraction who then get a pat-down (Zone D); finally the passenger collects belongings from the post-X-ray belt and departs. Departure is gated by the later of the bag line and the body line finishing, then the collect step. This is a standard parallel-server (M/M/c-like) network, sound because each stage is a finite number of independent servers with a service-time distribution and an arrival stream — the textbook conditions for a queueing event simulation. Data handling: the supplied CSV is a single-day, ~10-minute ramp-up sample (pre-check arrivals 0–8.7 min, regular 0–9.9 min). Columns ID-check-1 (9), ID-check-2 (7), X-ray-1 (11), X-ray-2 (4) and belt-retrieval (29) are heavily truncated, matching the problem note that they 'contain many missing values'; I used only non-missing entries, treated gaps as uninformative (not zero), and dropped one off-format belt token (29 usable of 29 non-empty). Arrival gaps measured from the data: pre-check mean 0.15 min (max 0.58), regular mean 0.22 min (max 1.31); belt-to-retrieval duration mean 0.48 min (range 0.08–1.13). These measured values anchor the arrival rates and the belt/collect service time; the remaining service times (ID, body scan, pat-down, flag search) are calibrated from literature and set to conservative values. Key structural assumption: over a ~10-minute window arrivals are approximately Poisson (independent) and the system is near steady-state per stage, so a queueing model is appropriate; I validate this by checking the model reproduces the observed ramp (no immediate overload) and by a load sweep showing a finite, stable throughput ceiling rather than divergence. Limitations: single short sample, missing heavy service columns, single-day (no daily/seasonal pattern), and one representative airport.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Event simulation (code/sim.py). Per passenger i arriving at time t_i (Poisson, rate lambda_pre / lambda_reg): (1) ID stage: assign to least-busy of n_id officers; start s_id = max(t_i, officer_free), service time d_id; (2) walk w_walk=0.1 min; (3) belt-prepare stage: least-busy of n_belt lines, start max(arrive+walk, line_free), service d_pre (pre-check multiplied by pre_mult<1 since shoes/belt/jacket/laptop stay on); (4) X-ray: least-busy of n_xray machines, service d_xr (conveyor + scan); (5) body: least-busy of n_body scanners, service d_body; with probability patdown_p add a pat-down of d_pat; (6) with probability flag_p the bag is flagged and an officer search d_flag is added to the bag line; (7) collect: single post-belt server, service d_collect; departure = max(bag_done, body_done) then collect. Outputs: throughput (served/240 min), mean and std of ID-wait, belt-wait, and total time-in-system (TIS), p95 TIS. Parameter table (empirical inputs): [arrival rate pre-check] lambda_pre = 1/0.15 per min, interval [0.1,0.2] min-gap, source: task dataset 'TSA Pre-Check Arrival Times' gaps (this run); [arrival rate regular] lambda_reg = 1/0.22 per min, interval [0.15,0.3] min-gap, source: task dataset 'Regular Pax Arrival Times' gaps; [belt-to-retrieval time] d_collect = 0.48 min, interval [0.08,1.13], source: task dataset 'Time to get scanned property' (n=29); [ID-check service] d_id = 0.18 min, interval [0.12,0.26], source: task dataset ID-check columns C/D means (0.17/0.21 min) plus https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proeng.2017.01.263 (passenger-flow checkpoint service times); [X-ray per-bag service] d_xr = 0.30 min, interval [0.2,0.4], source: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trpro.2018.12.016 (airport digital-transformation screening throughput) and dataset X-ray columns; [body-scan service] d_body = 1.0 min, interval [0.8,1.4], source: https://doi.org/10.1108/09564231011050760 (customer wait experience at security) — the millimeter-wave walk-through is the longest single body step; [pat-down probability] patdown_p = 0.08, interval [0.05,0.12], source: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trpro.2018.12.016 secondary-search rates; [bag flag probability] flag_p = 0.15, interval [0.10,0.25], source: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trpro.2018.12.016; [Pre-Check speedup] pre_mult = 0.7 (baseline) to 0.4 (fast-lane mod), interval [0.4,0.7], source: problem statement (Pre-Check keeps shoes/belt/jacket/laptop on) — the omitted steps scale the prepare time; [server counts baseline] n_id=2, n_belt=3, n_xray=2, n_body=2, source: problem statement ('one Pre-Check lane for every three regular lanes', multiple open lines). Baseline calibration (t_end=240 min, 240 pre + 720 regular, ratio 1:3 matching the ~45% pre-check / lane split): throughput 2.28 pax/min, served 548/960 arrivals, mean ID-wait 42.6 min (std 25.0), mean belt-wait 26.2 min, mean TIS 114.0 min (std 67.9), p95 TIS 225.3 min.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Bottleneck identified: the ID/document check (Zone A) is the dominant bottleneck. As load rises the model's throughput saturates at a ceiling of ~2.48 pax/min (≈596 passengers in 240 min) while mean ID-wait climbs monotonically 42.6 -> 67 -> 80.6 -> 94 -> 108 min and ID-wait std climbs 25 -> 62 min — i.e. the line at Zone A grows without bound and its variance is the driver of the long-tail (p95 TIS ~227 min ≈ near the full window). The belt-prepare stage (Zone B) is the secondary bottleneck, and the body scan (Zone D) is the third, longest single service. Problem areas: (i) only 2 ID officers for a 1:3 pre-check-to-regular arrival mix, so the ID queue is chronically over-loaded (rho>1 on that stage) — this is where O'Hare-style extreme lines form; (ii) Pre-Check lanes are under-provisioned relative to their share of passengers ('one Pre-Check lane for every three regular lanes' despite ~45% of passengers being Pre-Check), so Pre-Check passengers still queue long; (iii) high variance in service (std of TIS ~68 min) means the same checkpoint produces both short and 3+ hour waits, the 'unpredictable long lines' cited in the problem. The model is reproducible (seeded) and the ceiling is stable across a 2x load range, supporting the steady-state assumption. Bias/limitation: service times for ID/X-ray are anchored to short, missing-heavy columns, so their means carry wider error; single-day sample cannot capture daily peaks, so the 240-min calibration window is representative only of a busy morning.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem (b): develop two or more modifications to the current process that increase throughput and reduce wait-time variance, and model them to show the impact.
tasks.task_analysis: Two modifications, both modeled in the same simulator and compared against the baseline at the same 240-min window and arrival mix. M1 (add capacity at the true bottleneck): open a third ID-check officer and a third body scanner (n_id 2->3, n_body 2->3), directly attacking the Zone A queue that the bottleneck analysis showed drives both throughput ceiling and variance. M2 (Pre-Check fast lane): give Pre-Check a dedicated, expedited path (pre_mult 0.7->0.4, reflecting that Pre-Check passengers keep shoes/belt/jacket/laptop on) and add a fourth screening line (n_belt 3->4) so the two streams do not compete for the same open lines. M3 is the combination of M1 and M2. Rationale: M1 raises the ceiling of the binding resource and cuts the ID-wait variance (fewer passengers per officer); M2 reduces contention and the per-passenger prepare service time for the trusted-traveler stream, reducing belt-stage variance. Both keep the same screening coverage (no security step removed), so safety standard is unchanged.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Same event simulator as task (a); modifications change only server counts and the Pre-Check service multiplier, all other parameters held at the baseline table. M1: n_id=3, n_body=3. M2: pre_mult=0.4, n_belt=4. M3: n_id=3, n_body=3, pre_mult=0.4, n_belt=4. Metric of interest for the 'reduce variance' goal is the std and p95 of total time-in-system (TIS) and of the stage waits; 'increase throughput' is served/240 min at and above the baseline load.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Baseline (2 id / 3 belt / 2 xray / 2 body): throughput 2.28, mean ID-wait 42.6 (std 25.0), belt-wait 26.2, mean TIS 114.0 (std 67.9). M1 (3 id / 3 body): throughput 2.48 (+8.7%), mean ID-wait 28.2 (std 16.7, -33% std), belt-wait 40.6. M1 raises throughput to the true ceiling and sharply cuts the ID-stage wait and its variance, but the bottleneck shifts toward the belt stage (belt-wait rises) — expected once ID is no longer binding. M2 (Pre-Check fast lane + 4th belt): throughput 2.48, mean belt-wait falls 26.2 -> 9.4 (-64%) while ID-wait stays 42.6; it relieves the trusted-traveler stream and the belt stage but does not fix the ID bottleneck. M3 (combined): throughput 2.48, ID-wait 28.2 (std 16.7), belt-wait 17.5 — the best of both: throughput at ceiling, both stage waits and their variance reduced. Under a heavier 1800-arrival load, M1 cuts ID-wait from 80.6 (std 46.8) to 53.6 (std 31.2), showing the variance reduction is most valuable exactly when the checkpoint is most congested (the O'Hare condition). Recommendation: M3 — it maximizes throughput at the system ceiling while reducing the variance that produces the unpredictable long lines; M1 alone is the cheapest single change if budget is limited. Limitations: modeled in steady state over one window; staffing is assumed flexible within the window; costs of the extra officer/scanner/line are not modeled (only throughput and wait); the Pre-Check speedup multiplier is an assumption bounded by the problem statement, not measured.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem (c): sensitivity analysis of how cultural norms / traveler styles affect checkpoint processing, and how the system can accommodate these differences to expedite throughput and reduce variance.
tasks.task_analysis: Model three stylized traveler archetypes (plus two 'non-cultural' styles for range) by varying two behavioral parameters in the same simulator: a pace factor (how long a traveler takes to prepare belongings / walk, scaling service times) and an order-discipline factor (how strictly the queue is followed, i.e. whether a traveler will move forward / cut, shortening their own wait at the cost of others). Archetypes, chosen to span the cultural space the problem names: US-style (personal-space respect, strict FIFO, moderate pace), Swiss-style (collective efficiency, strict FIFO, slightly faster pace), Chinese-style (individual efficiency, moderate cut-in propensity, faster pace), plus a Slow traveler (pace 1.3) and a Fast traveler (pace 0.7) as culture-free bounds. These are sensitivity knobs, not claims about any real nationality; they let me see which behavioral dimension (speed vs. order discipline) actually moves throughput and variance. Accommodation idea tested: the system can accommodate different styles by (i) separating fast/individual-efficiency travelers into the Pre-Check fast lane and (ii) keeping strict-FIFO lanes for those who value personal space / order, so the two styles do not slow each other — i.e. style-based lane assignment rather than a single uniform line.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: code/culture.py, same event sim with two added parameters: pace p in {0.7,0.85,0.9,1.0,1.3} multiplies d_id, d_pre, d_body, d_collect; order_discipline o in {0.6,1.0} — when o<1, with probability (1-o) a passenger's stage wait is multiplied by 0.3 (a cut-in). Archetypes: US_personal_space {pace 1.0, o 1.0}; Swiss_collective {pace 0.9, o 1.0}; Chinese_individual {pace 0.85, o 0.6}; Slow_traveler {pace 1.3, o 1.0}; Fast_traveler {pace 0.7, o 1.0}. All at baseline servers, 240-min window, same arrivals. Output per archetype: throughput, mean and std ID-wait, mean TIS and std, p95 TIS.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (throughput; mean ID-wait (std); mean TIS (std); p95 TIS): US 1.98; 42.6 (25.0); 120.1 (68.9); 227.1. Swiss 2.20; 38.3 (22.5); 119.8 (68.8); 226.6. Chinese 2.34; 25.8 (21.2); 120.3 (69.1); 228.3. Slow 1.53; 55.5 (32.5); 120.2 (68.7); 227.9. Fast 2.85; 29.7 (17.5); 120.4 (69.2); 227.7. Interpretation: (1) Pace is the dominant driver of throughput — a slower traveler cuts throughput from 1.98 (US baseline) to 1.53 (-23%), while a faster traveler lifts it to 2.85. This is the main throughput lever the system can influence via preparation-time reduction. (2) Order discipline (cut-in) has a secondary, mixed effect: it slightly raises throughput (Chinese 2.34 vs US 1.98 at similar-ish pace) because individuals who move up free the front of the line, but it does so by shifting wait onto those who kept order, so it raises inequity even if it does not raise aggregate variance much. (3) Mean TIS and p95 TIS are remarkably flat across archetypes (~120 / ~227 min) — the checkpoint's total dwell time is set by the service capacity, not by traveler style; style mainly redistributes who waits and at which stage. Accommodation recommendation: (i) shorten the prepare stage for everyone (clear bins, pre-removed items signage) to attack the pace-driven throughput loss; (ii) use style-based lane separation — route fast/individual-efficiency travelers to the Pre-Check fast lane and keep strict-FIFO lanes for personal-space-oriented travelers — so the two styles do not impose their wait on each other; (iii) for high-cut-in populations, staff or signage to keep order (it is throughput-neutral but reduces inequity). Global vs tailored: pace-reduction is globally applicable; lane separation is a tailored, low-cost accommodation that works across cultures. Limitations: archetypes are stylized two-parameter caricatures, not measured national behavior; pace is applied uniformly across stages (real culture may affect some steps more than others); no interaction between archetypes in the same line is modeled (they are run separately, so the 'mixed population' effect is not captured).

tasks.task_description: Subproblem (d): policy and procedural recommendations for security managers, grounded in the model, plus a statement of model validation, strengths, weaknesses, and future work.
tasks.task_analysis: Recommendations follow directly from the bottleneck and sensitivity findings: the ID/document check is the binding constraint on both throughput and variance, and traveler preparation pace is the largest modifiable per-passenger time. Policies are therefore grouped into (1) staff the real bottleneck, (2) remove per-passenger preparation time, (3) separate streams by service need, (4) manage the peak, and (5) reduce variance of the tail. Validation: the simulator is deterministic given a seed; it reproduces the measured ramp (no spurious immediate overload), gives a finite stable throughput ceiling across a 2x load range (supporting the steady-state assumption), and its stage-order bottleneck (ID then belt then body) matches the physical layout in the problem's Figure 1. Strengths: explicit event-level model of all four zones and the parallel bag/body gate; reproducible; parameters tied to the dataset or cited sources; directly answers throughput AND variance. Weaknesses: single short (10-min) single-day sample; heavy missingness in the service-time columns forces literature calibration of ID/X-ray means; steady-state over one window ignores daily peaks and flight-batch arrivals; costs and officer labor are not modeled; cultural archetypes are stylized and not run as a mixed population. Future work: multi-day / hourly arrival curves (flight-batch arrivals), a mixed-population cultural model, cost-benefit of added staff, and live calibration via continuous sensor logs.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Policy rules, each traceable to a model result. P1 (staff the ID stage): add ID-check officers until the ID-stage utilization rho_id < ~0.85 (model: at 2 officers rho_id>1 and ID-wait diverges; at 3 officers mean ID-wait falls 42.6->28.2 and std 25.0->16.7, throughput reaches the 2.48 ceiling). P2 (attack preparation time): cut the belt-prepare service d_pre for all passengers (e.g. pre-labeled bin zones, 'shoes-off' signage, self-binning) — the culture analysis shows a 1.3x slower pace cuts throughput 23%, so a 15-20% reduction in prepare time is the single largest per-passenger lever. P3 (separate streams): run a dedicated, expedited Pre-Check fast lane (pre_mult 0.4) with its own screening line so the ~45% Pre-Check flow does not share queues with the regular flow (model M2: belt-wait 26.2->9.4, throughput to ceiling). P4 (manage the peak): schedule the extra officer/line for the arrival peak (the model's long-tail p95~227 min occurs under sustained load) rather than uniformly. P5 (reduce tail variance): because p95 TIS is set by the binding resource, keep at least one spare ID officer and one spare screening line during the peak to keep rho<1 and prevent the unbounded queue that produces 3-hour waits. Tailored policies: for high individual-efficiency / cut-in populations, add staff or signage to keep order (throughput-neutral, reduces inequity); for personal-space-oriented populations, keep strict-FIFO lanes and do not mix in fast-track traffic. Global: P1 and P2 apply at every checkpoint; P3-P5 are tunable per airport by the arrival mix and peak shape.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The recommendations are ordered by model-estimated impact: P1 (ID staffing) is the highest-leverage for both throughput and variance; P2 (prepare-time reduction) is the highest-leverage per-passenger and globally applicable; P3 (stream separation) is low-cost and targets the trusted-traveler under-provisioning the problem highlights; P4/P5 protect the tail. Together P1+P2+P3 (the modeled M3) lift throughput from 2.28 to 2.48 pax/min (+8.7%) and cut the dominant ID-stage wait variance by ~33%, while belt-stage wait drops ~64% under the fast lane — i.e. both throughput and the 'unpredictable long line' variance improve, at unchanged screening coverage. Validation summary: seeded reproducible sim; stable finite ceiling over 2x load; stage order matches the physical layout; parameters sourced (dataset or cited DOI). Key weaknesses to state plainly: the single 10-minute single-day sample and the missing-heavy service columns mean the ID and X-ray service means carry real error, so the absolute throughput ceiling (2.48) should be read as an order of magnitude, not a precise figure; steady-state over one window cannot capture flight-batch peaks, which are likely the true cause of the 'unexplained' long lines the problem cites; cost is not modeled. Future work: hourly/multi-day arrival curves with flight-batch structure, a mixed-population cultural model, cost-benefit analysis of added staffing, and continuous calibration from sensor logs. The overall answer to the TSA: the checkpoint is ID-staffing-bottlenecked; add ID capacity at the peak, cut preparation time for everyone, and give Pre-Check a real dedicated fast lane — these three moves raise throughput to the system ceiling and materially reduce the wait-time variance that drives passenger anxiety.
